title: Oak Village, and the tree that isn't there
where: The terraces where you started, between Lamble Street and Gordon House Road.
html:
You begin at a memorial to a missing tree. Gospel Oak takes its name from an oak that stood on the boundary between the parishes of Hampstead and St Pancras, near the corner of what is now Mansfield Road and Southampton Road. At the annual beating of the bounds — the parish walk that fixed the boundary in living memory before maps could be trusted — the procession halted at the tree and a passage of the Gospel was read over it. The oak was last recorded on a map in 1801 and had gone by some point in the nineteenth century. Oak Village, the little grid of cottages you set off from, is named for it.

Under your feet, the River Fleet. Its western branch rises on the Heath, comes down through the pond chain you will cross at stop 19, and runs culverted beneath Fleet Road and Southampton Road on its way to Blackfriars. It is the reason this valley was farmed rather than built on until the railways arrived.

The three landowners who shaped these streets were the Earls of Mansfield, Southampton and Lisburne. That first name matters for the rest of the walk: the Mansfields of Kenwood, whose house you reach at stop 7, owned the land you are standing on. Their surname is on Mansfield Road; their house's approach road is Gordon House Road. Serious building started in the mid-1800s and accelerated after Gospel Oak station opened in 1860 — confusingly named Kentish Town until 1867.

One street over Lissenden Gardens, the mansion-block estate on the far side of the railway, is where John Betjeman was born in 1906. He later wrote a poem called Parliament Hill Fields about the tram ride up Highgate Road.

title: Through the gate: how the Fields were bought
where: The Gordon House Road entrance, past the athletics track, climbing north-west.
html:
These 270-odd acres were nearly a housing estate. When the Metropolitan Board of Works bought the original Heath in 1871 (stop 5), Parliament Hill Fields was not included — it was farmland and parkland belonging to the Mansfield estate and its neighbours, and everyone understood it would be built over.

A public campaign, fronted by Baroness Burdett-Coutts and Octavia Hill, raised the money instead. The Hampstead Heath Enlargement Act of 1886 (amended in 1888) authorised the purchase; the Board adopted it in 1889, weeks before the Board itself was abolished and replaced by the London County Council. The price was £300,000 — a startling sum, roughly six times what the whole of the original Heath had cost eighteen years earlier — and it doubled the size of the open space at a stroke.

As you climb the eastern slope, look for the Stone of Free Speech, a low block of stone set in the grass. Its origins are murky, but it seems to have been a rallying point for open-air religious and political meetings around two centuries ago, and it is the reason the eastern flank of the hill has a long tradition of soapbox oratory. On the ground above it, George Whitefield is said to have preached in 1739, to draw a crowd away from the horse races then run on the Heath.

title: Parliament Hill — named by the losing side
where: The summit bench and the view indicator. Your watch logged 98.8 m here.
html:
Two stories compete, both seventeenth-century, and the second is the likelier.

The famous one: that Robert Catesby, Guy Fawkes and their fellow conspirators came here on 5 November 1605 to watch Parliament blow up. It is a lovely idea, and it is what gave the hill its older name of Traitors' Hill. But there is no contemporary evidence for it — the earliest printed versions are Victorian, and the conspirators had rather more pressing business that night.

The sober one: during the Civil War, troops loyal to Parliament occupied and fortified the high ground north of London, and this hill was one of the observation points. To Royalists it was Traitors' Hill; to the other side it was Parliament Hill. The name that stuck is the Parliamentarians'.

The view is legally defended. Parliament Hill holds one of London's protected strategic views, which is why the skyline in front of you has a conspicuous gap: developers cannot build into the sightline of St Paul's from this spot. The Palace of Westminster is visible too, which does no harm to the first story.

A footnote from the press In 1892 a boy digging on the hill is reported to have turned up coins and silver vessels valued at £2,000 — declared treasure trove and claimed by the Crown.

title: The Tumulus: Boudica's grave, minus Boudica
where: A railed, tree-covered mound a couple of hundred metres north-east of the path you took off the summit.
html:
Legend, tested and failed

A circular mound about 40 m across, ringed with iron railings and hawthorn. Victorian antiquarians decided it was the burial place of Boudica after her defeat by Suetonius Paulinus in AD 60 or 61, and the idea took hold so firmly that the sculptor of the Westminster Bridge Boudica group proposed siting his statue on top of it.

It was excavated in 1894. Nothing was found — no burial, no grave goods, nothing but domestic rubbish. The current best guesses are that it is either a genuine Bronze Age round barrow that was thoroughly robbed long ago, or, more prosaically, the raised mound of a seventeenth-century windmill. Neither has been proved.

The Heath does have real prehistory: Mesolithic flint tools have been found here, evidence of hunter-gatherers on this ridge around 7000 BC. Just not a queen.

title: The Viaduct ridge, and forty years of siege
where: The high ground crossing north-west towards Kenwood. The Viaduct and its pond lie in the valley below and to your left.
html:
This is the ground on which the whole Heath was won, and it is worth knowing the fight in detail because it is the most consequential thing that ever happened here.

The manor of Hampstead is old — Ethelred the Unready granted land at "Hemstede" to Westminster Abbey in 986, and it appears in Domesday. It passed into private hands in the twelfth century and, by 1767, into the Wilson family. In 1821 Sir Thomas Maryon Wilson inherited, and spent the next forty-eight years trying to build on it.

He was not a villain of the pantomime sort; he was a landowner with an entailed estate and a legally sound plan. He brought private bills before Parliament in 1829, 1830, 1843, 1844, 1853, 1854 and 1856. Every one was defeated or withdrawn. The 1856 attempt was overtaken by a general Act on settled estates that contained a clause, unprecedented and clearly personal, expressly barring him from using it.

Blocked in Parliament, he built anyway on land he held outright. From 1844 he threw a brick viaduct across the boggy valley below you — the foundation stone was laid in 1845 — as the spine of a carriage road serving 28 villas in the style of Regent's Park. He got a few courses of brick into the first villa. The excavations kept collapsing; the water kept coming in. The scheme died, and what survives is a handsome ornamental bridge over a handsome ornamental pond, carrying a road from nowhere to nowhere. It is the most eloquent ruin on the Heath.

Wilson died in 1869. His brother John, who inherited, had no appetite for the war. The Hampstead Heath Act 1871 let the Metropolitan Board of Works buy roughly 220 acres for £45,000 plus £2,000 in costs, on the statutory condition that it be "kept unenclosed and unbuilt on" for ever. Everything you walk over today descends from that sentence.

Why the Heath drains the way it does Underneath is London Clay, capped by Bagshot Sands and Claygate Beds. Water sinks through the sand, hits the clay and comes out sideways as springs — which is why there are ponds in every valley, why the sand was worth digging (stop 10), and why Wilson's villa foundations kept filling up.

title: Kenwood's south lawn: a bridge that is a painting
where: Below the house, by the water, before the final climb to the terrace.
html:
The dip your watch recorded here is the dam of the Thousand Pound Pond. At its far end sits the Sham Bridge: a wooden screen, painted and shaped to read as a three-arched bridge from the house, with nothing behind it. It is pure eighteenth-century scene-painting — a picturesque incident placed to close the view from the terrace.

Humphry Repton, the last of the great English landscape improvers, came to Kenwood on 8 May 1793 at the invitation of the 2nd Earl of Mansfield, and produced one of his celebrated Red Books — the watercolour before-and-after volumes that were his sales technique — in a matter of weeks. He moved the approach drives, resited the kitchen garden and stables, laid out a flower garden west of the house, and planted along the southern boundary specifically to hide Kentish Town. He also wanted the Sham Bridge removed, calling it beneath the dignity of Kenwood. He was overruled. It is still there, and it is now one of the best-loved things on the estate.

The lawns hold two twentieth-century interventions worth finding: Barbara Hepworth's Monolith (Empyrean) of 1953 and Henry Moore's Two Piece Reclining Figure No. 5 of 1964.

title: Kenwood House
where: The terrace and the Adam library. You stopped here for twenty minutes.
html:
A house called Caen Wood stood here from about 1616, built by John Bill, King's Printer to James I, and rebuilt around 1694 by William Bridges, Surveyor-General of the Ordnance. Everything that makes the building famous begins in 1754, when it was bought by William Murray, 1st Earl of Mansfield, Lord Chief Justice of England.

From 1764 Murray employed Robert Adam to remodel it. Adam added the Ionic portico and — his masterstroke — the library on the east end, built to balance the existing orangery on the west and to hold Murray's books. It is one of the finest surviving Adam interiors anywhere, a barrel-vaulted room with apsidal ends screened by columns, and it was designed, in Adam's own framing, as a room for both books and company.

Mansfield, Somerset, and Dido Belle

In 1772 Mansfield decided Somerset v Stewart, the case of James Somerset, an enslaved man brought to England who escaped and was seized to be shipped to Jamaica. Mansfield ruled that slavery was "of such a nature, that it is incapable of being introduced on any reasons, moral or political; but only positive law" — that is, it could exist only where a statute expressly created it, and no English statute did. He afterwards insisted the judgment settled only the narrow question of forcible removal, but abolitionists read it as holding that slavery could not exist on English soil, and it became one of the load-bearing texts of the movement.

Living in this house at the time was Dido Elizabeth Belle (1761–1804), the daughter of Mansfield's nephew Sir John Lindsay and Maria Belle, an enslaved African woman in the West Indies. Brought to England in 1765 and raised at Kenwood alongside her cousin Lady Elizabeth Murray, Dido lived here for some three decades in a position with no real precedent: she managed the dairy and poultry yards, and — far more unusually — took dictation for the Lord Chief Justice's correspondence, work normally done by a male secretary. A visitor in 1779, Thomas Hutchinson, recorded that she "was called upon by my Lord every minute for this thing and that."

The limits were real and should not be softened. She received £20 a year against Lady Elizabeth's £100; she did not dine with formal company, joining the ladies afterwards for coffee; and Mansfield's will, which confirmed her freedom and left her £500 and an annuity of £100, pointedly declined to name her as his niece. Lady Elizabeth got £10,000. A contemporary painting of the two young women together, long attributed to Zoffany and now generally given to David Martin (c. 1778), hangs in Scotland; Historic England calls it unique in eighteenth-century British art for showing a Black woman and a white woman as near equals. Dido married John Davinier in 1793 and died in Pimlico in 1804, aged 43.

Riot, bequest and theft

In June 1780 the anti-Catholic Gordon Riots engulfed London. Mansfield's Bloomsbury house was burned with his library in it, and a mob set out for Kenwood. The tradition — pub-owned but consistently told — is that the landlord of the Spaniards Inn (stop 8) stood the rioters free ale until cavalry arrived. The house survived.

The 2nd Earl added north wings by George Saunders; George III visited in 1794, William IV and Queen Adelaide in 1835. By the twentieth century the family had let the place out, to a Russian grand duke and then to an American heiress, and in 1922 the estate came onto the market for building. A Kenwood Preservation Council raised the money for 100 acres of the grounds, and 32 acres south of the mansion were opened to the public by George V in 1925.

The house itself was saved by beer. Edward Cecil Guinness, 1st Earl of Iveagh, bought Kenwood with 74 acres in 1925, filled it with sixty-three Old Masters from his own collection, and left the whole thing to the nation on his death in 1927. It opened as a public gallery in 1928. What hangs here — Rembrandt's late Self-Portrait with Two Circles, Vermeer's The Guitar Player, Hals, Gainsborough, Reynolds, Romney — is among the best collections in Britain, and it is free.

On the night of 23 February 1974 a thief cut the phone lines, smashed the shutters and a barred ground-floor window with a sledgehammer, took The Guitar Player and went over a ten-foot wall. The ransom note demanded that the IRA prisoners Dolours and Marion Price be transferred from an English prison to one in Ireland. Police long suspected Rose Dugdale, though she was never charged with it. The painting was recovered on 7 May 1974, propped against a gravestone in the churchyard of St Bartholomew the Great in Smithfield, wrapped in newspaper and tied with string. It was damp. It was otherwise fine.

  • c.1616Caen Wood House built by John Bill, King's Printer
  • 1754Bought by William Murray, 1st Earl of Mansfield
  • 1764Robert Adam begins the remodelling; the library follows
  • 1772Mansfield decides Somerset v Stewart
  • 1780Gordon Riots; Kenwood threatened, Bloomsbury house burned
  • 1793Repton's Red Book; Mansfield dies; Dido Belle leaves and marries
  • 1925–28Iveagh buys, dies, bequeaths; opens as a public gallery
  • 1974Vermeer stolen in February, recovered in May
  • 1986Passes to English Heritage on the abolition of the GLC

title: Hampstead Lane and the Spaniards Inn
where: Along Kenwood's northern edge. The inn and its tollhouse pinch the road 350 m to your north-west.
html:
The pub claims 1585, and stood at the entrance to the Bishop of London's estate — this was the boundary, and a boundary stone dated 1755 is still in the front garden. Opposite it, jutting into the carriageway, is the tollhouse of about 1710. The two buildings squeeze the road to a single lane, which is why a 1966 proposal to demolish the tollhouse was thrown out: removing it would have made the traffic worse, not better.

The name most likely commemorates a Spanish ambassador who lodged there, though several rival explanations circulate.

Legend

Dick Turpin. The pub says his father was landlord and that Turpin drank here. There is no documentary support for either claim. What is documented is that this stretch of road was genuinely dangerous — arrests for highway robbery nearby are recorded in 1751 — so the association is at least the right kind of story in the right place.

The literary tally is unusually long for one pub. Dickens put it in The Pickwick Papers, where Mrs Bardell is lured to the tea gardens. Bram Stoker used it in Dracula. Constable painted Road to the Spaniards, Hampstead in 1822. Galsworthy brought the Forsytes here. The pub's claim that Keats wrote Ode to a Nightingale in the garden is affectionate rather than accurate — he wrote it at Wentworth Place, a mile south-east.

title: Spaniards Road: a causeway on a sand ridge
where: The ridge road. Your track paused here for nearly two hours — the lunch of the Lunch Walk.
html:
You are on the spine of the Northern Heights, at 134 m the second-highest ground on the walk. The road runs along a natural sand ridge, and the reason it feels like a causeway — raised, with the heath dropping away on both sides behind avenues of trees — is that the land either side was quarried out from under it.

Sand digging was the Heath's industry. In 1813 the fine sand was reckoned to average ten feet in depth. The lord of the manor sold it by the cartload — about twenty cartloads a day around 1811 — and copyholders complained bitterly in 1806 that the pits were dangerous and had nearly destroyed the place. In 1866–67 the Midland Railway bought quarter-acre strips along Spaniards Road and dug 25 feet down. In 1924 the road was closed to motor traffic on either side and the flanking tracks became bridle paths.

Elms House Off the southern end of Spaniards Road stood Elms House, on the site of Mother Huff's tea garden (in business 1678–1728). Thomas Erskine, later Lord Chancellor, lived there 1811–19; it became St Columba's Hospital in 1957, was later owned by the Woolworths heiress Barbara Hutton, and was converted to flats in 1987.

title: Sandy Heath: the landscape that is an absence
where: West of Spaniards Road, in the pits and hummocks under the birches.
html:
Sandy Heath — the triangle between Spaniards Road and North End Way, known when the Board bought it in 1871 as North Heath — looks like ancient wild wood. It is not. Almost every hollow, bank and pond here is a quarry, and the ground level is many feet below where it used to be. This is a post-industrial landscape that has had 150 years to grow a wood over itself, and it is now among the quietest parts of the Heath. In 2021 Quiet Parks International gave Hampstead Heath "Urban Quiet Park" status; this is the corner that earns it.

Look for the Walter Field Memorial Fountain, put up in 1907 by the sister of the landscape painter Walter Field (b. 1837), who worked on the Heath. It is a listed structure and easy to walk past.

Beyond, to the north, lies the Heath Extension — 80 acres of Eton College's Wyldes farm, bought in 1907 after a campaign led by Henrietta Barnett, who then built Hampstead Garden Suburb up against it. She and her husband Samuel are commemorated with a blue plaque on Spaniards Road.

title: North End: a Prime Minister's breakdown and a music-hall song
where: The westernmost point of your walk, at the top of North End Way.
html:
A hamlet, then a resort, now barely a place at all. Three things happened here.

Pitt's seclusion. The merchant Charles Dingley invited William Pitt the Elder to North End in 1763 and rebuilt the house for him — a new wing, and a gymnasium for the children — by 1766, when Pitt moved in. Pitt was by then Earl of Chatham and, from 1766, effectively Prime Minister; in 1767 he collapsed into a severe depressive illness and withdrew here almost completely, refusing to see ministers and reportedly having meals passed through a hatch. The house was known variously as North End House, Wildwoods and finally Pitt House. It was demolished in 1952. An archway and a stretch of wall survive, in what is now called Pitt's Garden.

Wyldes Farm. Medieval land of the leper hospital of St James, bought by Eton College in 1449; the farmhouse dates from about 1600. The painter John Linnell moved his family here in the 1820s to escape London's air, and his visitors included William Blake — Linnell was Blake's patron in his last years, and it was Linnell who commissioned the Dante watercolours and the Job engravings. Charles Dickens stayed briefly in 1837, in the shattering weeks after the death of his sister-in-law Mary Hogarth. Raymond Unwin, co-planner of the Garden Suburb, lived there from 1906 to 1940. It survives as The Old Wyldes.

The Old Bull and Bush. A farmhouse by 1645, licensed to sell ale in 1721, with a music licence from 1867. Hogarth is said to have drunk here and to have had a hand in laying out the garden. It gave its name to the music-hall song made famous by Florrie Forde, which is why a pub on the edge of a heath is known to people who have never been to London.

The station that never opened Beneath you is North End station — "Bull and Bush" — begun for the Charing Cross, Euston and Hampstead Railway and abandoned at platform level when Henrietta Barnett's campaign stopped development above it. It would have been the deepest station on the Underground. In the 1950s the shell was fitted out as a control centre for the deep-tube flood gates. An emergency stair of 197 steps comes up on Hampstead Way.

title: West Heath and the Leg of Mutton Pond
where: Turning south through the woods. The pond lies about 100 m to your west.
html:
The Leg of Mutton Pond, named for its shape, was dug around 1816 — almost certainly as a make-work scheme. The Napoleonic wars had ended in 1815; demobilised soldiers and a collapsed war economy produced serious unemployment, and parishes across England responded by inventing earthworks. This is one of them: a piece of Regency welfare policy that is now simply a nice pond.

West Heath, between North End Way and West Heath Road, came into public hands with the rest in 1871. It is the least visited third of the Heath and the most wooded.

title: The Hill Garden and Pergola: soap money and tunnel spoil
where: The high point of the walk. The pergola runs 250 m along the ridge above West Heath.
html:
This is the strangest thing on the Heath and the best argument for a February walk, when the wisteria is bare and the structure reads as pure architecture.

William Hesketh Lever — Lever Brothers, Sunlight Soap, later 1st Viscount Leverhulme — bought The Hill in 1904 and hired the landscape architect Thomas Mawson. The problem was the site: to look out over the Heath rather than at it, the garden needed to be 20 to 30 feet higher than it was. The solution arrived by cart. The Charing Cross, Euston and Hampstead Railway was at that moment driving its tunnels out to Golders Green, opened in 1907, and Lever bought the spoil. The terraces you walk on are, in substance, the inside of the Northern line.

The first stage was finished in 1906 and Lever kept extending it for the rest of his life — buying adjoining land, adding a ballroom beneath the terrace in 1923, still building when he died in 1925. The result is a raised classical walk of columns, vaults and belvederes, laid out for a soap magnate's garden parties, with the wild heath immediately below it.

After Lever's death the house was bought by Andrew Weir, 1st Baron Inverforth, and renamed Inverforth House. He left it to Manor House Hospital in 1955; the London County Council took the gardens in 1960 and opened them to the public in 1963; the Corporation of London took over in the late 1980s and has been restoring the structure, which had been left to fall down, ever since. The house was sold to developers in the 1990s and is now flats.

The roof of inner London Your track's highest reading, 136.6 m, is on this ridge. The summit of the Heath just west of Spaniards Road, at 137 m, is the highest point in Inner London and was the highest point of the old County of London. It is not the highest point in Greater London — that is Westerham Heights in Bromley, at 245 m.

title: Whitestone Pond and Jack Straw's Castle
where: A 250 m detour east from where you crossed North End Way.
html:
The pond at 133 m was the Horse Pond: a place to water horses at the top of a long hard climb, and to soak wooden cartwheels so the timber swelled and the iron tyres stayed on. The vestry enlarged and lined it in 1856. Its present name comes from a milestone beside it reading "IV miles from St Giles, 4½ miles 29 yards from Holborn Bars".

Height made this ridge useful. Between 1808 and 1814 the Heath carried a station in the Admiralty's shutter telegraph chain — the semaphore relay that ran from Whitehall to Great Yarmouth, passing messages by line of sight in minutes rather than a day's ride. The little domed Hampstead Observatory, run by the Hampstead Scientific Society, still uses the same asset and is open to the public on clear winter evenings.

Jack Straw's Castle, on the corner, is named for the leader — with Wat Tyler and John Ball — of the Peasants' Revolt of 1381. The tradition is that he sheltered here before being taken and beheaded.

Legend

There is no evidence of a building on this site in 1381, and no record of a pub here before the early 1700s. But it was a proper coaching inn once the road mattered. Dickens came repeatedly, and wrote of coming up for "a red-hot chop for dinner, and a glass of good wine"; Thackeray and Wilkie Collins drank here; Stoker set a scene here in Dracula; Pinter used it in No Man's Land. It was wrecked by a bomb — reported in the Daily Herald on 29 March 1941 — and rebuilt in 1964 to a weatherboarded design by Raymond Erith, the classicist who also rebuilt the interior of 10 Downing Street. Betjeman called it "true Middlesex" and "a delight". It stopped being a pub in 2002 and is now flats and a gym, which is a sad end for the most literary inn on the hill.

title: Judges Walk, Upper Terrace and Constable's ground
where: The avenue along the top, before the drop into Hampstead Grove.
html:
An avenue of limes appearing on London maps from 1745. The name is attached to a story that during the Great Plague of 1665 the courts fled the City and sat in the open air up here, out of the infected air.

Legend, and probably late

No contemporary record supports it, and the walk was more plausibly named for judges who lived nearby or promenaded there. It is nonetheless the sort of story that Hampstead has always liked about itself: the hill as the healthy place, the refuge above the smoke. That belief is the engine of the next stop but one.

This is Constable country in a literal sense. John Constable took 2 Lower Terrace, just off here, in 1821, and painted this ground repeatedly — the pond at Branch Hill, the sand excavations, the firs, and above all the sky. He did his oil sketches of cloud formations on this ridge, annotating them on the back with the date, hour, wind direction and weather. It is the closest thing English painting has to a meteorological record.

title: Hampstead Grove: a quarterdeck and the oldest house
where: Between Admiral's House and Fenton House. You stopped here for half an hour.
html:
The street was simply "The Grove" when first recorded in 1831; it was renamed Hampstead Grove in 1937 to stop it being confused with The Grove in Highgate.

Admiral's House was built in 1700 by Charles Keys and originally called Golden Spikes — possibly because it served as a masonic lodge between 1730 and 1745. The naval captain Fountain North bought it around 1775, renamed it The Grove, and added the thing you cannot miss: a quarterdeck on the roof, with bulwarks and portholes. No admiral ever lived here. The name is an eighteenth-century error, apparently caused by confusion with Admiral Matthew Barton, another Hampstead resident who fired cannon from his own roof.

Constable painted it. George Gilbert Scott — St Pancras station, the Albert Memorial, some 800 buildings — lived here from 1856 to 1865 and decided Hampstead was too cold for him; his blue plaque went up in 1910. And it is the model for Admiral Boom's house in Mary Poppins: P. L. Travers lived in Hampstead, and the cannon-firing admiral came straight off this roof. The 1964 film shot here. In the adjoining Grove House, John Galsworthy wrote most of The Forsyte Saga between 1918 and 1933.

A few doors down is Fenton House, built in 1693 and the oldest surviving mansion in Hampstead — a plain, beautiful merchant's house of warm brick with a walled garden, sunken garden and an orchard of about thirty apple varieties. It was called Ostend House, then Clock House; the present name comes from Philip Fenton, a Riga merchant who bought it in 1793. Its last owner, Lady Binning, left it to the National Trust in 1952 along with her porcelain. It also holds the Benton Fletcher collection of early keyboard instruments — harpsichords, virginals, spinets, clavichords — which are kept in playing order and are played. If you hear a harpsichord through an open window, that is what it is. Grade I listed.

Also on this street: New Grove House, home of the artist and novelist George du Maurier, who wrote Trilby and gave the language the word "Svengali"; his son Gerald the actor, and thus his granddaughter Daphne, belong to the same house.

title: Flask Walk, Burgh House and Well Walk: the spa that built the village
where: Down Holly Hill and Heath Street, across the top of the village, then east along Well Walk to the Heath.
html:
Hampstead is a hilltop village that became fashionable because of iron in the water, and these three streets are the whole story.

The springs here are chalybeate — iron-bearing, faintly rusty, and in the seventeenth century believed to be medicinal. Celia Fiennes compared them to Tunbridge Wells and Bath in 1697. On 20 December 1698 the Earl and Countess of Gainsborough conveyed six acres of spring-bearing land to trustees for the benefit of Hampstead's poor, and the trustees promptly went into business. By 1700 the water was being advertised for sale at Charing Cross and Cheapside.

In 1701 John Duffield leased the land at £50 a year and built the apparatus of a spa: a Great Room for assemblies, partitioned to hold a pump room with a basin of the water; a tavern, a chapel, shops, formal gardens and a bowling green. Concerts and dances started in the summer of 1701. Dr John Arbuthnot took the waters in the Long Room in 1734, and Alexander Pope came to see him. The nearby Upper Flask tavern became a summer haunt of the Kit-Cat Club until it broke up around 1720.

It did not last. Scandal, unpaid rents and slack trustees killed the trade; in 1725 the Great Room was converted into a chapel, and the spa was effectively finished. The village it had drawn to the hilltop stayed.

  • Flask WalkNamed for the flasks the mineral water was bottled in, at the site of the present Flask pub, and sold across London under a seal of a wolf rampant with seven crosslets.
  • Well WalkThe spa's promenade. The 1882 memorial fountain marks the well; the original source, about 100 yards uphill, was filled in around 1880 and the new one never ran properly once the sewers went in.
  • Burgh HouseBuilt 1704. The spa's physician Dr William Gibbons moved in and enlarged it in 1720 — his initials are in the wrought-iron gate. Rudyard Kipling's daughter lived here 1933–37, and his last outing, in 1936, was to visit her. Now Hampstead Museum. Grade I.

John Constable lived at 40 Well Walk (renumbered from 6) from the summer of 1827 until his death in 1837, and painted London from its windows. His grave is in the churchyard of St John-at-Hampstead on Church Row, five minutes west. In 1774 Roman pottery was dug up in this street, which has led to a long-running and unresolved argument about whether a Roman road ran over the hill.

title: East Heath and the Vale of Health
where: Out across the East Heath. The Vale lies in its hollow 400 m to your north-west.
html:
This open ground was the East Park — the 60 acres Maryon Wilson held freehold and fought hardest to build on, and where the Viaduct scheme was aimed. On it stands the Pound, built in 1787 to impound stray pigs, with a keeper, John Stevenson, to run it. It is the most ordinary structure on the Heath and the one that most directly records what a common was actually for.

In the hollow to the north-west is the Vale of Health, a hamlet entirely surrounded by heath. It was a boggy patch called Gangmoor, and then, after a harness-maker named Samuel Hatch put up a workshop around 1714, Hatch's or Hatchett's Bottom. In 1777 the Hampstead Water Company enlarged the pond and drained the marsh; cottages for the poor followed in 1779. The name "Vale of Health" first appears in 1801 and is, by all appearances, an estate agent's euphemism that worked.

What followed was one of the densest literary clusters in London. Leigh Hunt lived here from 1815 to 1819, straight out of prison for libelling the Prince Regent, and his cottage became the meeting place for the second generation of Romantics: Byron and Shelley both came, and Keats — who lived at Wentworth Place, now Keats House on Keats Grove, a mile south-east — was Hunt's protégé. Coleridge and George Crabbe were in the Vale between 1825 and 1832. Later came Rabindranath Tagore (1912), D. H. Lawrence (1915), Stella Gibbons (1927–30, working on Cold Comfort Farm), and Compton Mackenzie (1937–43), who called it "village life half an hour from Piccadilly Circus".

'Appy 'Ampstead From the 1860s the Vale had a hotel, tea gardens and a fairground, and the East Heath held bank-holiday fairs on a scale now hard to imagine: 30,000 people on an August Monday in the 1870s, 50,000 on a fine Whit Monday, an estimated 200,000 on Easter Monday 1910. Hampstead Heath station opened in 1860 and brought the East End up by the trainload. In 1892 nine people died in a crush escaping a thunderstorm.

title: The Hampstead Ponds: London's water supply
where: The dip in your profile — crossing the dams of the Hampstead chain.
html:
These are not natural lakes. They are reservoirs, built in a chain down the valley of the Fleet's western branch, and the dams are the paths you walk on.

The springs here were earmarked for London's supply as early as 1543. In 1692 Parliament created the Hampstead Water Company to exploit them, and it dammed Hampstead Brook in stages through the eighteenth century — two ponds by 1703, three by 1745, four by 1810 — building what are now the Mixed Bathing Pond, Hampstead No. 2 and Hampstead No. 1. A steam pumping engine worked below No. 1 from the 1830s until 1907. In 1856 the New River Company bought the Vale of Health Pond, the Viaduct Pond and Hampstead No. 1 for drinking water, at a time when contemporaries were describing the Vale of Health pond as weed-choked and receiving sewage. Drinking use ended before 1900. There are eighteen ponds on the Heath today.

Swimming came in sideways: informal immersion in the early 1800s, formalised at the Mixed Pond by 1884. The Highgate Men's Pond, on the other chain, opened on 1 May 1893. The Kenwood Ladies' Pond opened in June 1926 and is still the only women-only open-water bathing pond in Europe; it marked its centenary in 2026. In 2005 the High Court settled a long fight with the Corporation by ruling that adults could swim unsupervised at their own risk, which is why the ponds are open all year without lifeguards on the water at dawn.

The dams are also, unglamorously, statutory reservoirs above a densely populated valley. The Corporation rebuilt them for safety between 2014 and 2016, to considerable local fury and a generally good result.

title: The Lido, and back to the oak
where: Past the Lido and the athletics track, out of the Fields, and east into Oak Village.
html:
Parliament Hill Lido opened on 20 August 1938, designed by Harry Rowbotham and T. L. Smithson of the London County Council Parks Department. At £34,000 it was the most expensive of the thirteen lidos the LCC built between 1920 and 1939 — an unmistakable piece of municipal ambition, dropped at the working-class end of the park where the fairground crowds came off the trains. It was listed Grade II in January 1999 and given a stainless steel lining in 2005, the first outdoor pool in Britain to get one. It is unheated, which regular swimmers regard as the point.

Then the Fields' south gate, and Oak Village. Behind you is a landscape that was defended in Parliament seven times, bought twice by public subscription, quarried for sand, dammed for drinking water, painted by Constable, walked by Keats, guarded by the copyholders who wouldn't let their lord enclose it, and finally passed — after the Metropolitan Board of Works, the LCC and the GLC — to the City of London Corporation, which has run it since 1989. Sheep came back in 2019 and again in 2023.

The oak the whole district is named after is still missing.
